steps: Examine UT-AIR (Plant air compressor) tags header_pressure_bar and compressor_current_a around the stop time. A sustained drop in header_pressure_bar below 6.0 bar while compressor_current_a remains near or above 100 A supports a massive header leak or compressor delivery failure; normal header pressure (6.0 to 7.5 bar) with normal compressor cycling refutes a central plant compressed air supply failure.

Examine ST20-WLD (Weld cell A) tag air_pressure_bar around the stop event. A drop below normal operating range (5.3 bar) while UT-AIR header pressure is normal supports a localized pneumatic leak, regulator malfunction, or isolation valve issue at ST20; normal pressure (5.3 to 5.9 bar) refutes a local air pressure loss at ST20.

Compare ST30-WLD (Weld cell B) tag air_pressure_bar with ST20-WLD air_pressure_bar leading up to the stop. Concurrently depressed air pressure at ST30-WLD supports a common header branch or plant-wide utility drop; normal pressure at ST30-WLD while ST20-WLD is low refutes a shared distribution header issue and isolates the failure to ST20-WLD.

Evaluate whether ST20-WLD air_pressure_bar data anomaly is a sensor or data problem rather than a physical pneumatic failure. Check ST20-WLD air_pressure_bar telemetry for sudden zero-readings, frozen values, transmitter disconnect flags, or inconsistency with pneumatic clamp motion; erratic or out-of-range sensor readings without pneumatic actuator stall support an instrumentation/sensor failure, whereas gradual pressure decline consistent with cylinder stall refutes a sensor fault.

Check ST10-PRS (Press) tags cycle_time_s and hyd_pressure_bar leading up to the stop. Extended cycle times or hydraulic pressure drops at ST10 would support upstream part starvation or process delays triggering the line hold; nominal cycle times (45 to 54 s) refute an upstream mechanical bottleneck from the press.

Examine ST20-WLD tags weld_current_ka and tip_resistance_mohm on cycles immediately preceding the stop. Increased tip resistance or weld faults consistent with weak clamp force support low pneumatic clamping pressure; normal weld electrical characteristics refute weld tip degradation or weld controller electrical faults.

citations.quote: A sustained fall in header pressure while the compressor runs loaded indicates demand exceeding supply, most often a distribution leak.
When leakage plus demand exceed what the compressor can deliver, the compressor stays loaded, header pressure falls below the cut-in pressure, and the 5.6 bar low alarm (A-UTAIR-HDR-LO) follows.

| Header pressure falling, compressor loaded continuously | Distribution leak (drop legs, couplings, hoses) or a new air user | Ultrasonic leak survey of the header and the ST20/ST30 drop legs with the cells stopped | Repair the leaks; confirm the header holds pressure (see Table 3-2) |
If the combined total of line leakage and weld cell demand exceeds compressor output capacity, the unit remains loaded continuously without reaching 7.3 bar.

citations.quote: Regulated gun air (`air_pressure_bar`) normally sits at 5.6 bar within 5.3 to 5.9 bar. Below 5 bar the cell raises a low-air alarm; at 4.6 bar the supply-air interlock stops the cell. Gun force alarms (A-ST20-GUN-FRC, A-ST30-GUN-FRC) can appear as the air falls.

When gun air pressure falls at ST20 and ST30 together, the cause is upstream in the plant air supply; check the header pressure (see Section 6.2 of AM-CA-01 (Plant Air System and Utilities)) before working on either cell.
When gun air falls at one cell only, check that cell's filter-regulator, drop-leg ball valve and quick couplings.

| Gun air low at one cell only | Filter-regulator element clogged, regulator drifted, or local leak | Read the cell gauge; listen for leaks at the drop leg and couplings | Replace the filter element; reset the regulator; repair the leak |
